lead: he still gets the letters. seven years on, the thing you and he made in that back room is asked about by everyone, and the asking goes to him, because he is the one who stayed with it.
sun: the work is not in question. it was good, it carries your name, and people who were not born when you finished it can tell you whose it is. what never got arranged is the rest — who holds the master, who answers when a stranger writes, who says yes to the reprint. those are things a person sets up while still caring, and you were already gone.
moon: the appetite that made it was for a question, and the thing answered the question. inside a season you were following something else entirely, honestly, with no sense of having left anything behind — a finished thing does not smell of anything. so the years when its fate was being decided were years you spent elsewhere, at full attention, on something new and unrelated.
pull: your name is on it and his is on the correspondence. he did not take anything. he was simply still standing there when the questions started, and you were four rooms away.
tension: at parties he explains how it was done, in front of you, and gets a detail wrong that changes who thought of what. the room hears an old friend being fond. correcting it would turn seven years of him keeping the thing alive into a theft he never committed, so you let it stand, again, and the friendship now runs on a version of the past you do not privately hold.
cost: you can hand a finished thing to whoever is nearest and go, which is why there are a dozen of them and most people manage two. the friend who stayed is not a lesser person for having stayed. he owns the account of the best year of your life, he came by it honestly, and you were not in the room when it changed hands.

lead: four sentences you said standing up at a launch are on the back of every edition since, in your name, and the man they were about has built eleven years on them. you meant all four.
sun: you were asked to speak because of what you make, and the room takes a verdict from someone whose own work is that good as though it had been checked. nothing was checked. you said the warm accurate thing without the qualifier a careful person attaches — no on this evidence, no for now, no terms of any kind — because attaching one has never occurred to you at the moment of speaking.
moon: a sentence delivered at that volume does not come back down to a working size later. it went out whole, in front of eighty people, and it is quoted now by strangers who were not there. the same evening you said nothing at all about the woman sitting two along, and that has been just as durable, and she has read it correctly for eleven years.
pull: a verdict you cannot revise and did not know you were issuing went out that evening. it is on his covers, in his funding applications, and it will be read out at his funeral.
tension: his last three books have been thin and he knows it too, and the sentence goes on the back of each without anyone asking you. permission was never the mechanism — the thing is out and you are not the sort of person who writes to a publisher about a quotation. saying it fresh is the only currency you have left, and the year you do not say it will be the year he finds out what you think.
cost: one true sentence from you, said out loud in a full room, has started careers, and it works because everyone can see you have no interest in being owed. the sentence is now a fixed object with your name on it, doing work you stopped agreeing with around its fourth year, and the only way to withdraw it is a silence loud enough to end him.

lead: nine years out, and the sign over the door still has your name on it, kept there out of real fondness. what nobody checked, on the way back in, was whether the name still came with a vote.
sun: what you left behind was finished and good and known to be yours, which is exactly why it did not need you. nine years of other people running it well, your name over all of it, said with affection at the front of every introduction. no clause was ever written down, because writing one would have meant imagining a day when the thing you made and the people in it were on different sides.
moon: leaving never got filed as an ending, so nothing was arranged for an absence, because an absence with a return in it does not look like a risk from the inside. and the second time did arrive, warm: a welcome, a seat at the table, your picture on the wall by the stairs. all of it real, all of it ceremonial, none of it attached to anything that moves.
pull: you came back to the honour version of your own work. they are delighted you are here, the delight is genuine, and nothing in the building answers to you.
tension: the first time you say the standard has slipped, it arrives as a founder being sentimental about the old way, and three people move to reassure you before you have finished the sentence. asking for anything firmer now — a seat with a vote, a say over what still goes out as yours — would read as coming back to collect. so you are consulted, warmly, twice a year, and everything you said is thanked for.
cost: nine years of absence did nothing to it, which is a fact about how well it was made and about nothing else. most builders cannot leave a thing standing; you can, and did, twice. the welcome was genuine and they meant every word of it. the place with your name over the door is the one room where your opinion arrives as a courtesy.

lead: the thing you made after he died is the best work of your life, and it is where everyone else goes to be sad about him. The Ghost put no edge on it and nobody has looked for one.
sun: grief here comes out as craft, the only channel open, and what came out was accurate and beautiful and unmistakably yours. everybody knows whose hands it was. it also went out the way everything else does — finished, on show, with no note about who it was for. so the most private thing you have ever done is a public object, and the day it opened was the day it stopped being yours.
moon: what looked like one object turns out to be feeding a crowd nobody counted — his colleagues, two ex-wives, people who met him twice, arriving to be fed by something you built out of your worst year. they are not wrong to come. the asking has no edge on it either: a copy, a speech every anniversary, the key, a photograph for a piece somebody is writing.
pull: his people have one place to go and you made it, and you have not been in it alone since it opened. your grief is the exhibit; everyone else is the visitor.
tension: nobody has asked how you are, because the object is composed and you are assumed to be the same. the version of him it carries is theirs to adjust now, and they do. stopping any part of it would read as taking him back off the people who loved him, and that is the one accusation you would not survive. so the anniversary happens, and you are at the door of it, receiving.
cost: a death in your circle produces something that outlasts everybody's memory of him, made well enough that people who never met him stand in front of it and get something. your mourning went in entire and came out as an object with an opening night. what is left of him anywhere is a room with your name on the plaque and his in the title.
